paragraphs: And at that “tragic” phrase Grushenka broke down. She hid her face in her hands, threw herself onto the sofa cushions and sobbed like a little child.
Alyosha got up and went over to Rakitin.
“Misha,” he said, “don’t be angry. She hurt you, but don’t be angry. Did you hear what she just said? You mustn’t ask too much of human endurance. One has to be merciful.”

Alyosha said this because his heart prompted him to, without thinking. He felt he had to speak, and he turned to Rakitin. If Rakitin hadn’t been there, he would have spoken to the empty air. But Rakitin gave him a mocking look, and Alyosha stopped short.
“You were stuffed so full of your elder’s teaching last night that now you have to unload it on me, Alexey, man of God!” said Rakitin, with a hateful smile.

“Don’t laugh, Rakitin, don’t smile, and don’t talk about the dead. He was better than anyone in the world!” cried Alyosha, with tears in his voice. “I wasn’t speaking to you as a judge, but as the lowest of the judged. What am I next to her? I came here looking for my own ruin, and I told myself, ‘What does it matter?’ out of cowardice. But she has suffered for five years, and the moment anyone says a word to her from the heart, she forgets everything and forgives everything, in her tears! The man who wronged her has come back and sent for her, and she forgives him everything and hurries joyfully to meet him, and she won’t take a knife with her. She won’t! No, I am not like that. I don’t know whether you are, Misha, but I am not like that. It’s a lesson to me.... She has more love in her than we have.... Have you ever heard her say before what she has just told us? No, you haven’t. If you had, you’d have understood her long ago ... and the person who was insulted the day before yesterday must forgive her, too! She will, once she knows ... and she shall know.... This soul isn’t yet at peace with itself. One must be tender with it ... there may be a treasure in that soul....”
Alyosha stopped, because he had run out of breath. Bad mood or not, Rakitin looked at him in astonishment. He had never expected such a speech from gentle Alyosha.
“She’s found someone to plead her case! What, are you in love with her? Agrafena Alexandrovna, our monk is really in love with you. You’ve made a conquest!” he cried, with a coarse laugh.
Grushenka raised her head from the pillow and looked at Alyosha, a tender smile shining on her tear-stained face.

“Leave him alone, Alyosha, my cherub. You see what he is. He’s not someone you should talk to. Mihail Osipovitch,” she turned to Rakitin, “I meant to ask your pardon for being rude to you, but now I don’t want to. Alyosha, come to me, sit down here.” She beckoned to him with a happy smile. “That’s right, sit here. Tell me,” she shook him by the hand and peeped into his face, smiling, “tell me, do I love that man or not? The man who wronged me, do I love him or not? Before you came, I was lying here in the dark, asking my heart whether I loved him. Decide for me, Alyosha. The time has come, and it shall be as you say. Am I to forgive him or not?”
“But you have forgiven him already,” said Alyosha, smiling.

“Yes, I really have forgiven him,” Grushenka murmured thoughtfully. “What a miserable heart! To my miserable heart!” She snatched a glass from the table, emptied it in one gulp, held it up in the air and flung it on the floor. The glass broke with a crash. A small cruel line appeared in her smile.

“Perhaps I haven’t forgiven him, though,” she said, with a kind of menace in her voice, and she dropped her eyes to the ground as if she were talking to herself. “Perhaps my heart is only getting ready to forgive. I’ll fight with my heart. You see, Alyosha, in these five years I’ve grown to love my tears.... Perhaps I only love my resentment, not him ...”
“Well, I wouldn’t like to be in his shoes,” hissed Rakitin.
“Well, you won’t be, Rakitin. You’ll never be in his shoes. You shall black my shoes, Rakitin. That’s the place you’re fit for. You’ll never get a woman like me ... and he won’t either, perhaps ...”
“Won’t he? Then why are you dressed up like that?” said Rakitin, with a venomous sneer.

“Don’t taunt me about dressing up, Rakitin. You don’t know everything that’s in my heart! If I choose to tear off my finery, I’ll tear it off at once, this minute,” she cried in a ringing voice. “You don’t know what that finery is for, Rakitin! Perhaps I’ll see him and say, ‘Have you ever seen me look like this before?’ He left me a thin, sickly little crybaby of seventeen. I’ll sit beside him, fascinate him and work him up. ‘Do you see what I’m like now?’ I’ll say to him. ‘Well, that’s all you’re getting, my dear sir. There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip!’ That may be what the finery is for, Rakitin.” Grushenka finished with a spiteful laugh. “I’m violent and I hold grudges, Alyosha. I’ll tear off my finery, I’ll destroy my beauty, I’ll scorch my face, slash it with a knife, and turn beggar. If I choose, I won’t go anywhere now to see anyone. If I choose, I’ll send Kuzma back everything he has ever given me, tomorrow, and all his money, and I’ll go out scrubbing floors for the rest of my life. You think I wouldn’t do it, Rakitin? That I wouldn’t dare? I would, I would, I could do it right now, only don’t push me ... and I’ll send him about his business, I’ll snap my fingers in his face, and he’ll never see me again!”
She screamed the last words hysterically, then broke down again, hid her face in her hands, buried it in the pillow and shook with sobs.
Rakitin got up.
“It’s time we left,” he said. “It’s late, and we’ll be locked out of the monastery.”
Grushenka leapt up from her place.

“Surely you don’t want to go, Alyosha!” she cried, in mournful surprise. “What are you doing to me? You’ve stirred up my feelings, you’ve tortured me, and now you’ll leave me to face this night alone!”
“He can hardly spend the night with you! Though if he wants to, let him! I’ll go alone,” Rakitin scoffed.
“Quiet, you evil tongue!” Grushenka cried angrily at him. “You never said to me the words he came to say.”
“What did he say to you that was so special?” asked Rakitin irritably.

“I can’t say, I don’t know. I don’t know what he said to me, but it went straight to my heart. He has wrung my heart.... He is the first, the only one who has pitied me, that’s what it is. Why didn’t you come before, you angel?” She fell on her knees in front of him as if in a sudden frenzy. “I’ve been waiting my whole life for someone like you. I knew someone like you would come and forgive me. I believed that, nasty as I am, someone would really love me, not only with a shameful love!”
“What have I done to you?” answered Alyosha, bending over her with a tender smile and gently taking her by the hands. “I only gave you an onion, nothing but a tiny little onion, that was all!”

He was moved to tears himself as he said it. At that moment there was a sudden noise in the passage, and someone came into the hall. Grushenka jumped up, looking greatly alarmed. Fenya ran noisily into the room, crying out:

“Mistress, mistress darling, a messenger has galloped up,” she cried, breathless and joyful. “A carriage from Mokroe for you, Timofey the driver, with three horses. They’re just putting in fresh horses.... A letter, here’s the letter, mistress.”

She had a letter in her hand and she waved it in the air the whole time she talked. Grushenka snatched the letter from her and carried it to the candle. It was only a note, a few lines. She read it in one instant.
“He has sent for me,” she cried, her face white and twisted, with a wan smile. “He whistles! Crawl back, little dog!”
But she stood hesitating for only one instant. Then suddenly the blood rushed to her head and brought a glow to her cheeks.

“I will go,” she cried. “Five years of my life! Good-by! Good-by, Alyosha, my fate is sealed. Go, go, leave me, all of you, don’t let me see you again! Grushenka is flying to a new life.... And don’t you hold anything against me either, Rakitin. I may be going to my death! Ugh! I feel as if I were drunk!”
She suddenly left them and ran into her bedroom.
“Well, she has no thoughts for us now!” grumbled Rakitin. “Let’s go, or we may hear that female shrieking again. I’m sick of all these tears and cries.”

Alyosha let himself be led out like a sleepwalker. In the yard stood a covered cart. The horses were being taken out of the shafts, and men were running to and fro with a lantern. Three fresh horses were being led in at the open gate. But when Alyosha and Rakitin reached the bottom of the steps, Grushenka’s bedroom window was suddenly flung open and she called after Alyosha in a ringing voice:

“Alyosha, give my greetings to your brother Mitya, and tell him not to hold it against me, though I have brought him misery. And tell him this too, in my words: ‘Grushenka has fallen to a scoundrel, and not to you, noble heart.’ And add that Grushenka loved him only one hour, only one short hour she loved him—so let him remember that hour all his life—say, ‘Grushenka tells you to!’”
She ended in a voice full of sobs. The window shut with a slam.
“H’m, h’m!” growled Rakitin, laughing. “She murders your brother Mitya and then tells him to remember it all his life! What ferocity!”

Alyosha made no reply. He seemed not to have heard. He walked fast beside Rakitin as if in a terrible hurry. He was lost in thought and moved like a man in a trance. Rakitin felt a sudden twinge, as if someone had touched an open wound. By bringing Grushenka and Alyosha together he had expected something quite different. Something very different from what he had hoped for had happened.

“He’s a Pole, that officer of hers,” he began again, holding himself in. “And really he’s not an officer at all now. He served in the customs in Siberia, somewhere on the Chinese frontier, some puny little beggar of a Pole, I expect. Lost his job, they say. Now he’s heard that Grushenka has saved a little money, so he’s turned up again. That’s the explanation of the mystery.”
Again Alyosha seemed not to hear. Rakitin couldn’t control himself.

“Well, so you’ve saved the sinner?” he laughed spitefully. “Have you set the Magdalene on the right path? Driven out the seven devils, eh? So you see, the miracles you were looking out for just now have come to pass!”
“Hush, Rakitin,” Alyosha answered, with an aching heart.
“So you despise me now for those twenty-five roubles? You think I’ve sold my friend. But you’re not Christ, you know, and I’m not Judas.”
“Oh, Rakitin, I assure you I’d forgotten about it,” cried Alyosha. “You’re the one reminding me of it....”
But this was the last straw for Rakitin.
“Damn the lot of you, every one!” he cried suddenly. “Why the devil did I ever take you up? I don’t want to know you from now on. Go alone, there’s your road!”
And he turned abruptly into another street, leaving Alyosha alone in the dark. Alyosha came out of the town and walked across the fields to the monastery.
